377.t: Debut as accompanist: nightclubs rather than vaudeville pits
377.s: Basie disputes Feather's 'professional debut in New York accompanying vaudeville acts', saying he accompanied acts in nightclubs but never played a theater pit, and refuses to name early gigs.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City
377.q: Well, I don't know how to just go through all this. I mean, I don't -- I hate to just do anything about how? He's got the thing written there.

377.t: Nightclub work then vaudeville in New York, never in a pit
377.s: Kuehl tries to pin down the order of his early work; Basie says Feather's statement is true but misplaced as a debut.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City
377.q: Well, maybe he meant later years, too, maybe he's speaking about later years, when I came to New York with my band.

377.t: Replacing Fats Waller in Katie Crippen's act; June Clark and Sonny Greer
377.s: Basie confirms replacing Waller in a traveling vaudeville act, and working with trumpeter June Clark and Sonny Greer, partly in New York.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City
377.q: Some of it. Some of it not. That (inaudible). Some of them was in New York, some was in (inaudible) another place.

377.t: Mrs. Holloway, Asbury Park, Leroy's, and June Clark
377.s: Basie confirms lessons with Mrs. Holloway, summers in Asbury Park and playing at Leroy's in New York, but says he never worked with Elmer Snowden.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City

631.t: The Musical Rubes in New York vaudeville and band's breakup
631.s: Brown's band played vaudeville as Musical Rubes; song pluggers applauded and the band broke up.
631.ch: Brown's Band in Chicago and New York
631.q: Well, how'd that come about? Well, uh, That was out of New York? That was in New York, yes. Uh-huh. So they, you see, the uniform originated in Chicago at the Lambs, so that musical rubes. Oh, yeah, to dress up and... Oh, sure, sure. They figured that they put a lot of corn shocks and a haystack…

10.t: New York winters and the move to New Orleans
10.s: Carew recalls hearing music and vaudeville in New York, his acrobat ambition, and how he came to New Orleans in 1904.
10.ch: Early life and New Orleans arrival
10.q: Before I went to New York, yes. But I kept it up there. I, I, I bought music there. I used to go down to Segal Cooper's was a very big popular department store then. And I'd listen to the demonstrations there and buy music then. And, uh. Did you hear any ragtime players in New York? No. Any of you…

639.t: The Academy of Music band and vaudeville tour
639.s: He remembers a Dixieland band heard in New York, later playing trumpet in a vaudeville act, and the difficulty of returning to jazz at WSMB.
639.q: No, no. Except, uh, I was in the Academy of Music, you know, on 14th Street one day. Yeah. And I heard a jazz band that just knocked me completely unconscious. It was a knockout. Now that could have been Red Nichols, uh, uh, I don't think Bix had come to town that early.

581.t: Arriving in New York in 1954 and playing the Apollo
581.s: The duo comes by train to Harlem, is booked at the Apollo, and Mr. Schiffman tells them to cut the jokes.
581.ch: Detroit and the Bop and Locke act
581.q: But we got booked into the Apollo Theater which was unheard of. That was one of the biggest Vaudeville houses that’s ever been. And we didn’t have no name. We only had played once in Detroit. And this agent saw us there. And we played at the Colonial Theater. And then he submitted us to the Apollo.…

145.t: With Hampton 1940-42; the Apollo and Stokowski
145.s: Royal's two years with Hampton, huge Apollo crowds on their first New York visit, and Stokowski found waiting in line.
145.ch: Hampton and Basie: tours and road life
145.q: I was with Hampton from the end of -- from the fall of 1940 until October, '42, we did our things. We had a great success when we first went to New York. We had such enormous crowds and at the Apollo Theater in Harlem, at our first showing there, we had people standing a half a block in line in…

26.t: Rooming with Duke and the Wilbur Sweatman vaudeville engagement
26.s: Greer and Duke share rooms at his aunt's, then the group gets work with Wilbur Sweatman on Keith's circuit, made up to look light-skinned.
26.ch: New York, the Kentucky Club and the high-hat
26.q: "You know what you're doing." I say, 'Man, New York's my town, don't worry about it. New York's my town." I knew Willie "the Lion" and Lucky and all them guys, and in the meantime I used to go there and rehearse every Sunday. I belonged to the Clef Club. That was big, that was big like the union is…

89.t: Clarence Potter and his Jazz Babies, a flop in Hoboken
89.s: His first New York contact was singer Clarence Potter, who imitated Harry Lauder; their act was so bad the Hoboken manager just paid carfare.
89.q: with musicians was a fellow by the name of Clarence Potter. He heard about this clarinet player from Ohio -- it was a big joke -- This Clarence Potter was a very dark Negro who had sharp, sharp features and he did Scottish imitations. He imitated Sir Harry Lauder. He sang in Scotch, he did the…
